meta.title: Knivchit: screenshots with annotations for GNOME on Wayland
meta.description: Early preview of Knivchit, a screenshot tool for GNOME on Wayland. Rounded selection, arrows, text and a mosaic brush; copy, save or pin the result. Local only, no accounts, no telemetry.
meta.ogTitle: Knivchit: screenshots with annotations for GNOME
meta.ogDescription: Select, annotate and pin your screen on GNOME with Wayland. Local only, no accounts, no telemetry.

hero.h1: Screenshots with annotations, built for GNOME on Wayland
hero.sub: Knivchit freezes your screen, lets you draw a rounded selection, mark it up with arrows, text and mosaic, then copy, save or pin the result. Everything stays on your machine.
hero.meta: v{{VERSION}} does one thing: screenshots. Expect rough edges and breaking changes, and back up anything you care about. Tested on GNOME 50. Free and open source.

how.h2: From screen to clipboard in three steps
how.intro: The capture happens on a frozen copy of your screen, so nothing moves while you choose.

steps.title: Press your shortcut
steps.text: You pick the key combination in Settings; Knivchit doesn't assign any. The screen freezes and dims.

steps.title: Select and annotate
steps.text: Drag a box, adjust it with the handles and mark what matters from the toolbar.

steps.title: Copy, save or pin
steps.text: Copy the image, save it to your folder, or leave it floating on screen while you work.

stage.alt1: Diagram of the first step: the dimmed screen with a rounded selection box and the hint to drag to select.
stage.alt2: Diagram of the second step: the selection with an arrow, a rectangle and a mosaic area, and the toolbar below.
stage.alt3: Diagram of the third step: the cropped capture floating over the desktop and a notice that it was saved and copied.
stage.hint: Drag to select · Esc to cancel
stage.toast: Saved and copied to the clipboard

tools.h2: Eight tools, each with its own cursor
tools.intro: Pick them from the toolbar or the keyboard: <kbd>Alt</kbd> plus the letter always works, even while you type text; the bare letter works when you aren't typing.
tools.colors: Six annotation colors. Keys are matched by physical position, so they work on any keyboard layout. The letters follow the Spanish tool names for now, because the interface is in Spanish.

list.name: Select
list.text: Touch a shape to move or resize it.

list.name: Rectangle
list.text: Frame a button, a paragraph or an error.

list.name: Ellipse
list.text: Circle what you want to point out.

list.name: Arrow
list.text: Point at an exact spot in the image.

list.name: Pen
list.text: Freehand strokes, to underline or cross out.

list.name: Text
list.text: Type a note straight onto the capture. Editable afterwards, with alignment.

list.name: Mosaic
list.text: Paint over what shouldn't be seen: passwords, names, addresses.

list.name: Eraser
list.text: Remove a drawn shape you don't want to keep.

edit.intro: What you draw stays editable until you finish the capture.

points.title: Move and resize
points.text: With Select you drag any shape and resize it from its corners, or move one end of an arrow. The capture selection itself also moves and resizes with eight handles.

points.title: Undo and redo
points.text: <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> <kbd>Z</kbd> undoes the last stroke and <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> <kbd>Shift</kbd> <kbd>Z</kbd> brings it back.

points.title: Mosaic as a brush
points.text: Mosaic is painted like a thick stroke, not a box, so you cover only what you need to hide.

points.title: Native resolution
points.text: The crop and the annotations are composed at your screen's real resolution, not the preview's.

edit.pinNote: A pinned capture is a borderless window you can drag. Keeping it above other windows needs the GNOME Shell extension to be active.

why.intro: On Wayland, GNOME decides what an application may do. Knivchit is built around that instead of fighting it.

points.title: Made for modern GNOME
points.text: On Wayland a regular app can't register global shortcuts, place its own window or stay above others. A small GNOME Shell extension does exactly that and nothing else; the app does the rest.

points.title: Careful design
points.text: A rounded selection, matching dark and light themes, and motion that respects your reduced-motion setting. The page you're reading uses the same tokens as the app.

points.title: Predictable
points.text: It captures once and works on that image, so what ends up in the file is what you saw when you pressed the shortcut.

settings.intro: Knivchit ships with no global shortcut. You record one in Settings and it warns you if it clashes with a GNOME one. The main window is a narrow column on the right of the screen; the extension places it, because on Wayland an app can't position its own window.

points.title: Record any combination
points.text: Press the keys you want while recording. The result is applied through the extension, so it works across GNOME.

points.title: Dark, light or system
points.text: The app follows GNOME's preference or the one you set. This page does the same.

points.title: Your save folder
points.text: Choose where captures land (the default is a Knivchit folder inside Pictures) and open it from Home. Launching at login is optional and off by default.

privacy.h2: Your screen stays on your machine
privacy.intro: Knivchit has no server, no accounts and no cloud. What you capture goes to the folder you choose or to the clipboard, and nowhere else.

items.title: No accounts, no telemetry
items.text: There is no sign-up and no usage statistics are sent. This page has no analytics or cookies either.

items.title: No network unless you ask
items.text: The app's only connection is “Check for updates” in About, and only when you click it. The extension never uses the network.

items.title: The extension does the minimum
items.text: It registers the shortcut you chose, keeps pinned windows on top and places the main window. It doesn't read the clipboard or what you type.

items.title: The keyboard, only while recording a shortcut
items.text: While you record a combination the extension grabs the keyboard for a few seconds to read it. Only the final combination is used, and the grab is always released: when done, on Esc, on a click or on timeout.

items.title: Clipboard history will be off by default
items.text: It doesn't exist yet. When it arrives it will be opt-in, and its contents will never be written to logs.

privacy.license: The app is MIT licensed and the GNOME Shell extension is GPL-3.0-or-later.

soon.h2: From screenshot tool to digital Swiss Army knife
soon.intro: Today Knivchit does one thing: screenshots. The plan is to bring together what currently takes several separate tools. None of the following exists yet, and there are no dates.

list.name: Clipboard history
list.text: Get back what you copied earlier, search it and paste it again.

list.name: Text from the screen (OCR)
list.text: Extract the text from any area of the screen instead of retyping it.

list.name: Translation
list.text: Translate that text without leaving what you're doing.

list.name: Emoji panel
list.text: A quick picker to insert emoji.

list.name: Stickers
list.text: Browse and insert stickers from the same panel.

soon.visual: The capture toolbar already reserves their place, disabled.

install.intro: Two pieces: the app (an AppImage) and a GNOME Shell extension.
install.alphaStrip: Early preview, not stable yet. Expect rough edges and breaking changes, and back up anything you care about.
install.noRelease: No release published yet. These commands apply from the first release.

req.title: Requirements
items: Xwayland (on by default in Fedora and Ubuntu).
req.language: The app's interface is in Spanish for now (English planned).

script.title: With the script
script.intro: Downloads the latest release (a pre-release while no stable one exists), verifies the checksums and installs the app and the extension.
script.command: curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kevincharp/knivchit/main/install.sh -o install.sh && less install.sh && bash install.sh
script.read: Opens the script in less first; press q to continue. --stable requires a stable version; --version v0.1.0-alpha.2 pins one.
script.after: It prints “installing PRE-RELEASE …” first. When done, log out and back in once, then assign your shortcut in Settings.

steps.title: Download
steps.text: AppImage, extension zip and SHA256SUMS from the release page.

steps.title: Install the extension
steps.code:
gnome-extensions install --force knivchit-extension-*.zip
gnome-extensions enable knivchit@knivchit.dev

steps.title: Run the app
steps.text: Run it, log out and back in once, then assign your shortcut in Settings.

list.a: No. Knivchit is an early preview (alpha). There are no compatibility guarantees between versions: settings and data may be migrated or reset, and things can break. Back up anything you care about, and report problems through issues. While no stable release exists, the installer picks the latest pre-release (--stable refuses that).
list.repoLinked: No. Knivchit is an early preview (alpha). There are no compatibility guarantees between versions: settings and data may be migrated or reset, and things can break. Back up anything you care about, and report problems through issues. While no stable release exists, the installer picks the latest pre-release (--stable refuses that).

list.q: Does it work on KDE, X11 or other desktops?
list.a: Knivchit is designed and tested for GNOME on Wayland only. Other desktops and X11 sessions are untested, and nothing is promised there.
Tested on GNOME 50 on Wayland. The extension declares support for 50 only; widening that means testing each version first.

list.q: Why does it need a GNOME Shell extension?
list.a: On GNOME with Wayland an app can't register global shortcuts, place its window or keep another one on top. Only GNOME Shell can, and the extension is limited to exactly that.

list.q: Is it safe? What can it access?
list.a: The app has no server and makes no network requests except “Check for updates”, when you click it. The extension doesn't use the network or read the clipboard, and it grabs the keyboard only while you record a shortcut. The installer verifies SHA-256 sums before installing anything. Both the app and the extension are open source.
In the folder you pick in Settings. The default is a Knivchit folder inside your Pictures directory. Copying to the clipboard doesn't write a file.
Run bash install.sh --uninstall. It removes the app, the service, launch-at-login and the extension. Your captures stay where they are.

list.q: Why is the interface in Spanish?
list.a: The project started in Spanish and the app has not been translated yet. An English interface is planned; there is no date.

list.q: How do I report a bug or suggest an idea?
list.a: Open an issue with the bug or feature template. Knivchit is issues-first: the maintainer handles issues, and pull requests are only accepted for an issue that was approved first, or for very small fixes.
list.repoLinked: Open an issue with the bug or feature template on GitHub. Knivchit is issues-first: the maintainer handles issues, and pull requests are only accepted for an issue that was approved first, or for very small fixes.

list.a: The app is MIT; the GNOME Shell extension is GPL-3.0-or-later; the site and docs are MIT.
The repository isn't public yet. When it is, the link will appear on this page.
list.repoLinked: The code is in the public repository.

list.q: Will there be clipboard history, OCR or emoji?
list.a: That's the intention, which is why they appear under “Coming soon”. Today they don't exist and there's no date.

contribute.intro: Knivchit is issues-first and has a single maintainer with limited time.

points.title: Open an issue
points.text: The normal way to help is to open an issue with the bug or feature template. The maintainer fixes it.

points.title: Pull requests, by invitation
points.text: A PR is accepted only against an issue the maintainer has approved, or for a very small, self-contained fix such as a typo. Larger PRs without an approved issue are closed unreviewed, and there's no promise of a fast review.

points.title: Security problems
points.text: Report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting, never in a public issue.
